name: Arbitrariness
definition: The tie between a signal and its meaning is conventional rather than a resemblance.
source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

name: Broadcast Transmission And Directional Reception
definition: The signal radiates to any receiver in range, and a receiver can locate its source.
source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

name: Discreteness
definition: The signal is built from a repertoire of distinct units, so a small deviation either switches units outright or is heard as a noisy version of the same one.
source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

name: Displacement
definition: Messages can be about things remote in time or space.
source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

name: Duality Of Patterning
definition: A small stock of meaningless units combines into a large stock of meaningful ones.
source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

name: Interchangeability
definition: Any user who can understand a message can also produce it.
source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

name: Learnability
definition: A user of one such system can learn another.
source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

name: Prevarication
definition: Messages can be false, deceptive or meaningless.
source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

name: Productivity
definition: Messages never sent before can be produced and understood.
source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

name: Rapid Fading
definition: The signal does not persist. Unlike a track, a spoor or a written record, it is gone once transmitted and will not wait for the hearer's convenience.
source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

name: Reflexiveness
definition: The system can be used to communicate about itself.
source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

name: Semanticity
definition: Signals carry fixed associations to things and situations in the world.
source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

name: Specialization
definition: The signal exists in order to communicate, rather than being a side effect of some other behaviour.
source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

name: Total Feedback
definition: The sender perceives everything relevant in their own signal.
source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

name: Traditional Transmission
definition: The system is learned from other users rather than inherited genetically.
source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).

name: Vocal-Auditory Channel
definition: Signals are made with the vocal tract and received by the auditory system.
source: Hockett, C. F. (1960). The Origin of Speech. Scientific American 203(3), 88-96. Features 14-16 were added in Hockett & Altmann (1968).
